title: Workplace Situational Judgement
src: Amazon SDE Intern OA 2026 · section 3 (scenarios written for this mock)
body:
For each scenario, pick the response you would most likely take. The real section covers teamwork and communication, ownership and customer focus, handling disagreement, taking feedback and decision making, and it maps onto Amazon's Leadership Principles.

The real OA's scenarios weren't shared, so these are original ones in the same style. Scoring: 2 points for the best answer, 1 for a partly good one, 0 otherwise.

items.s: Two days before a release, you notice that the new checkout flow adds an extra confirmation screen. It passes every test, but in a quick hallway trial three colleagues found it confusing. Your manager is in back-to-back meetings.
o: Mention it at the next sprint retrospective after the release.
Write up what you saw with screenshots, send it to your manager and the product owner, and propose a small fix you could finish before the release.
Ship as planned. It meets the spec and the tests pass.
Remove the screen yourself and push the change without telling anyone, since it is clearly better.
items.why: Raise the customer problem early, with evidence and a concrete fix, and keep the decision makers informed. Changing scope silently skips the people who own the release.

items.s: While fixing your own bug you find a second bug in a shared library owned by another team. It doesn't affect your feature yet, but it will corrupt data for two other services.
o: File a detailed ticket with the owning team, message their on-call with the impact, and offer a patch if they want one.
Patch the library in your branch and merge it with your feature.
Tell your manager and let them decide whether to raise it.
Ignore it. It belongs to another team.
items.why: Owners act beyond their own code: make sure the right team knows, show the impact, and offer help, without bypassing their review.

items.s: In a design review the senior engineer picks a caching approach you believe will fail under peak load. You have a rough benchmark that supports your view. The team is leaning towards their option.
o: Share the benchmark, explain the risk calmly, and suggest a short load test. If the team still chooses their design, commit to it fully.
Stay quiet. They have more experience.
Agree in the meeting, then build your own version on the side.
Keep arguing until they agree with you.
items.why: Disagree with data and respect. Once a decision is made, commit to it instead of undermining it.

items.s: A production alert fires at night: 5% of image uploads are failing. A rollback of today's deploy is documented and safe, but you are not certain the deploy caused it.
o: Page the whole team and wait for someone senior before doing anything.
Start rewriting the upload service to make it more robust.
Wait until morning so you can investigate properly with the team.
Roll back using the runbook, confirm the error rate drops, post an update in the incident channel, and keep investigating.
items.why: When an action is reversible and documented, take it quickly to protect customers, then communicate and dig into the cause.

items.s: A dashboard shows that conversion went up 12% after your change. The jump looks too large for such a small tweak.
o: Quietly drop the metric from your report in case it is wrong.
Announce the result. The dashboard is the official source.
Check the raw events, the time window and whether tracking changed in the same deploy before you share the number.
Share it, but add a note that it might be wrong.
items.why: When a number doesn't match what you would expect, check the underlying data before you rely on it.

items.s: You realise that a config change you made last week caused a small outage that the team blamed on a network blip.
o: Fix the config quietly so it doesn't happen again.
Tell only your manager in private.
Say nothing. The incident is closed and no one was hurt.
Tell the team what happened, add it to the incident notes, and propose a check that would have caught it.
items.why: Admitting mistakes openly and fixing the process builds trust. A quiet fix helps, but the team keeps the wrong root cause.

items.s: Halfway through a sprint you realise you will miss a committed deadline by three days because an API you depend on is late.
o: Tell the stakeholders now, explain why, and offer options: a reduced first version on time, or the full version three days late.
Blame the other team in the stand-up.
Wait until the deadline and explain then.
Work late every night and hope you catch up.
items.why: Flag risks early and give the stakeholders options, so they can decide with time to spare.

items.s: You are given a ticket in a part of the codebase that uses a framework you have never used. The ticket is due in four days.
o: Ask a teammate to write it while you watch.
Ask to swap the ticket with someone who knows the framework.
Copy a similar file and change it until it works.
Spend a few focused hours on the framework docs and existing code, ask a teammate for a 15-minute walkthrough, then start.
items.why: Learn what you need, use teammates well, and still own the task.

items.s: A teammate asks you to approve a pull request today. It works, but it has no tests and repeats a block of logic that already exists in a helper.
o: Leave specific review comments: reuse the helper and add tests for the edge cases. Offer to pair on it so it can still merge today.
Reject it with the comment 'needs work'.
Approve it. They are under time pressure.
Approve it and open a follow-up ticket for the tests.
items.why: Keep the quality bar, but make your feedback specific and help the teammate get there.

items.s: Your team wants to add a new paid monitoring tool for a service that gets about 50 requests a day. The existing logging system could cover this with a small alert rule.
o: Suggest an alert rule in the existing system first, and set a clear signal for when a dedicated tool would be worth it.
Write your own monitoring tool from scratch.
Say nothing. It's not your budget.
Buy the tool. Monitoring is always worth it.
items.why: Solve the problem with what you already have, and keep the larger option open for when it is needed.

items.s: In your mid-internship review your mentor says your updates in stand-up are too long and hard to follow.
o: Agree, but keep doing it the same way.
Explain that the work is complex and needs the detail.
Thank them, ask for an example, and try a three-line format (done, next, blocked) from the next stand-up. Check back in a week.
Stop giving updates unless someone asks.
items.why: Take feedback openly, turn it into a concrete change, and follow up to check it worked.

items.s: Two teammates disagree in the team chat about how to name an API field. The thread is getting heated and has blocked your work for a day.
o: Post a joke to lighten the mood and move on.
Suggest a 15-minute call, summarise both options and the trade-offs, and agree on who makes the final decision.
Wait for them to sort it out.
Pick the name yourself and push the change.
items.why: Move the discussion to a short, structured conversation and agree who decides, so the work can continue.
